### Title: Algorithmic Price-Fixing in Multifamily Housing: The Antitrust Dilemma of YieldStar

Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies in restraint of trade. For over a century, antitrust jurisprudence has required evidence of a 'meeting of the minds' or conscious parallel conduct among competitors to prove an illegal price-fixing conspiracy (*Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly*, 2007). However, the widespread adoption of centralized revenue management software—most notably RealPage's YieldStar algorithm—has exposed a critical blind spot in classical antitrust frameworks by automating horizontal collusion through a third-party intermediary.

Traditionally, competing landlords in a local housing market set rents independently based on individual vacancy rates and localized supply-demand conditions. YieldStar disrupted this by pooling proprietary, non-public transactional lease data from thousands of participating property management companies. The algorithm ingests daily unit-level lease rates, concessions, and occupancy numbers to generate daily pricing recommendations. RealPage's software pricing advisors actively discourage leasing agents from deviating from algorithmic prices, maintaining compliance rates above 90%.

The economic effect of this centralized pricing coordination is the artificial restriction of housing supply. In a competitive market, a landlord with vacant units lowers rents to attract tenants. YieldStar's algorithm, however, calculates that maximizing total revenue across a market often requires keeping certain units vacant while hiking rents on remaining units. By outsourcing their pricing decisions to a single algorithm fed with shared proprietary data, competing landlords effectively form a hub-and-spoke cartel without ever speaking to one another.

In 2024, the Department of Justice and several state attorneys general filed antitrust lawsuits against RealPage, asserting that substituting an algorithm for a smoke-filled room does not make price-fixing legal. This litigation represents a foundational test case for antitrust in the algorithmic era: whether Section 1 liability can attach when the agreement is mediated not by direct horizontal communication, but by mutual algorithmic delegation.
